pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–9 years

- **Topic:** Heating & Cooling Changes

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y4 'States of matter'):** Pupils should be taught to "observe that some materials change state when they are heated or cooled, and measure or research the temperature at which this happens in degrees Celsius (°C)." Non-statutory guidance: "note the changes to water when it is heated or cooled"; research melting/condensing temperatures (e.g. when iron melts, when oxygen condenses); explore the effect of temperature on chocolate, butter, cream. Note: teachers should AVOID materials where heating causes chemical change (baking, burning).

- **Standards — US (NGSS 2-PS1-4):** "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-4]." Clarification: reversible examples include water and butter at different temperatures. DCI PS1.B: "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-4]." SEP: Engaging in Argument from Evidence.

- **Operational details:** Establish the two reversible state changes for water — melting (solid→liquid) and freezing (liquid→solid) — plus boiling/evaporation, and tie each to a MEASURED temperature: water freezes/melts at 0°C and boils at 100°C. Have children read a thermometer in °C and record the temperature at which a change happens, so the abstract change is pinned to a number. Use gentle everyday examples (chocolate, butter, ice) and explicitly keep to physical, reversible changes, avoiding burning/cooking. Confront the melting–dissolving confusion head-on (ice melting is heat-driven state change; sugar dissolving is a different process). The particle-level 'why' (heating gives particles more energy to move) is a light bridge to KS3, not the KS2 core, which is observe-and-measure.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C (observational→early-quantitative). The child can describe melting and freezing with everyday examples, state that water freezes at 0°C and boils at 100°C, read a thermometer in °C to record where a change occurs, and keep melting distinct from dissolving.
bestPractices: Pin every state change to a MEASURED temperature in °C (water: 0°C freeze/melt, 100°C boil), so children read and record, not just watch.
Teach melting and freezing as the same reversible boundary crossed in opposite directions (0°C for water).
Explicitly separate melting from dissolving — a classic conflation — with side-by-side examples (ice melting vs sugar dissolving).
Keep to physical, reversible changes and avoid heating that burns or cooks (chemical change), per DfE guidance.
Use thermometer-reading practice as a genuine measurement skill, discussing units and scale.
Reference researched melting/boiling points of other materials (iron melts very hot; oxygen condenses very cold) to show every material has its own change temperatures.
keyRepresentations: A thermometer scale in °C with 0°C (ice/water) and 100°C (boiling) marked
A melt↔freeze reversible-boundary diagram for water
A heating timeline: ice → water → steam with the temperatures of change
A materials-and-their-change-temperatures table (water, chocolate, iron, oxygen)
commonMisconceptions: Confusing melting with dissolving (thinking ice in a drink 'dissolves', or that melting needs a liquid to melt into).
Believing melting/boiling temperatures are vague or variable for a given substance, rather than fixed (water always 0°C / 100°C at normal pressure).
Thinking 'cold' is a substance that flows into things, rather than cooling being the removal of heat energy.
Assuming heating always makes new materials (over-generalising to chemical change) instead of many heating/cooling changes being reversible state changes.
Thinking a material must 'soften' gradually with no particular temperature, missing the idea of a specific melting point.

learn.summary: For ages 7–9: observe that some materials change state when heated or cooled, and pin each change to a MEASURED temperature in °C (pure water melts/freezes at 0°C and boils at 100°C at normal atmospheric pressure). Core skill is observe-and-measure: read a thermometer and record the temperature where a change happens. Some mixtures, such as chocolate, soften and melt over a range of temperatures rather than at one sharp point. Keep melting distinct from dissolving, keep to physical reversible changes (avoid burning/cooking), and show that melting and freezing are the same boundary crossed in opposite directions. Particle-level 'why' is a light bridge, not the core.

activities.title: Heat-and-cool bench: watch the change track the temperature
feedback: If the child expects the change at any warm temperature, draw attention to the marker landing at the same °C every run.

Point out that the reading pauses at the change temperature while the change happens (0°C during melting, 100°C during boiling) and only climbs again once the change is complete — the same sticking behaviour the real melting-ice task shows.

If the child calls melting 'dissolving', use the side-by-side panel: melting needs only heat and one substance; dissolving needs a second substance (a liquid the solid spreads into) and does not need heating, although warming can make it happen faster.
When reversing the dial re-freezes the water, confirm it is the SAME water, only the state changed — the change runs both ways.
activities.rationale: Live coupling of a readable number to a visible change makes the fixed-temperature idea concrete and lets the learner read-and-record rather than only watch; showing the reading hold at the change temperature keeps it coherent with the real-thermometer task. Reversibility and the melting-vs-dissolving contrast are built into the same model. A real thermometer and ice-water is the natural hands-on partner. (Proposed design; efficacy untested.)
sourceClaims: DfE Y4 'States of matter' statutory: 'observe that some materials change state when they are heated or cooled, and measure or research the temperature at which this happens in degrees Celsius (°C)'; avoid heating causing chemical change.
NGSS 2-PS1-4 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-4]'; DCI PS1.B '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-4]... sometimes reversible, sometimes not.'
Elementary misconceptions include melting/dissolving confusion, treating 'cold' as a substance, and not grasping fixed change temperatures; conceptual change needs hands-on, repeated observation.
learnerActions: Drag a heat dial under a beaker of ice and watch a thermometer climb in °C.

Notice the ice stays solid as the temperature rises, and observe that it begins to melt at 0°C, with a marker snapping onto the scale at that reading; the reading holds at 0°C while there is still ice melting.
Keep heating: once all the ice has melted the water warms to 100°C, where the reading holds while the water boils, with a marker at 100°C.
Reverse the dial to cool: watch steam recondense and the water refreeze at 0°C, showing the change runs both ways.
Use a side panel to run melting ice next to dissolving sugar and describe how the two processes differ.
Swap the material (chocolate, iron, oxygen) to discover each has its own change temperature or range (chocolate softens and melts gradually over a range of temperatures, not at one sharp point).
activities.intendedInsight: For water, melting, freezing and boiling do not happen vaguely 'when it gets warm': they happen at specific, readable temperatures (0°C and 100°C at normal atmospheric pressure) that are the same every time. The reading pauses at that temperature while the change is happening, and melting/freezing are the same boundary crossed in opposite directions. (Evaporation is different: it can happen slowly at temperatures below boiling.)

activities.title: Real thermometer in melting ice: predict the sticking point
feedback: A prediction of a steady climb signals the child hasn't grasped that energy first goes into changing state — use the observed sticking at 0°C to address this.

The 0°C plateau only shows while there is still unmelted ice in the beaker; use ordinary water ice as a melting ice-and-water mixture (never dry ice, which is frozen carbon dioxide, not water). Ice straight from the freezer may first read below 0°C and climb to 0°C, then hold there while it melts.
If the child says the melt-water is a new liquid, refreeze it to recover the ice and note the mass is unchanged (in a covered container, so none evaporates): same material, only the state changed.
activities.rationale: A predict–observe–explain task with a real thermometer makes the fixed melting point and the energy-goes-to-state idea observable, and the diagnostic prediction exposes misconceptions before teaching.
sourceClaims: Elementary misconceptions include melting/dissolving confusion, treating 'cold' as a substance, and not grasping fixed change temperatures; conceptual change needs hands-on, repeated observation.
learnerActions: Put a thermometer into a beaker of crushed melting ice (a genuine ice-and-water mixture), stir gently and let it warm slowly (for example in a warm room or with gentle warming), reading the temperature aloud.
Before starting, predict what the thermometer does WHILE the ice is still melting, and say why.
Observe whether the reading climbs steadily or sticks, and record the temperature where it holds.
Afterwards, refreeze the melt-water and check it is the same water (e.g. mass stays the same if the container is covered so no water evaporates).
activities.intendedInsight: While a melting ice-and-water mixture still has ice in it the temperature holds at about 0°C (the energy first goes into changing state), then climbs once all the ice has melted; the melt-water is the same material as the ice.

activities.title: Melting is not dissolving — and freezing is heat leaving
feedback: If the child uses 'dissolve' for ice becoming water in a warm room, contrast: dissolving needs a second substance the solid spreads into; melting does not.
If the child says the freezer 'puts cold in', reframe: heating ADDS energy (melt, boil), cooling REMOVES it (freeze); 'cold' is just less heat, not a thing that moves in.
If melted chocolate is called a new material, note it hardens back to the same chocolate when cooled — a reversible change of state.
activities.rationale: These are the classic KS2 conflations (melting/dissolving, change-of-state/new-material, cold-as-substance); confronting them head-on with side-by-side contrasts supports conceptual change.
sourceClaims: Elementary misconceptions include melting/dissolving confusion, treating 'cold' as a substance, and not grasping fixed change temperatures; conceptual change needs hands-on, repeated observation.
learnerActions: Compare ice melting in a warm room with sugar dissolving in water, and say what is different about each.
State which process needs heat and which needs a second substance.
Explain what happens when water freezes: does cold go IN, or does heat come OUT?
Decide whether melted chocolate is a new material or the same chocolate.
activities.intendedInsight: Melting is a heat-driven change of state of ONE substance; dissolving spreads a solid into a second liquid and does not need heating (though warming can speed it up). Freezing is heat energy leaving, not 'cold' moving in; a melted material is still the same material.

activities.title: Every material has its own change temperatures
feedback: If the child treats water's melting and boiling points as vague or variable, point to the fixed values (pure water always 0°C/100°C at normal atmospheric pressure), while noting that some mixtures such as chocolate do soften over a range.
When reading the scale, discuss the units (°C) and the spacing between marks so reading is accurate.
Iron, oxygen and boiling water are read/research examples only, not materials to handle at those temperatures.
activities.rationale: Referencing researched change temperatures of other materials generalises the fixed-temperature idea and gives genuine thermometer-reading practice, consistent with the measure-or-research standard.
sourceClaims: DfE Y4 'States of matter' statutory: 'observe that some materials change state when they are heated or cooled, and measure or research the temperature at which this happens in degrees Celsius (°C)'; avoid heating causing chemical change.
learnerActions: Read a table of materials and their change temperatures (water, chocolate, iron, oxygen).
Note that iron melts very hot and oxygen condenses very cold, while water melts at 0°C and boils at 100°C.
Place 0°C and 100°C correctly on a thermometer scale and read other values off it.
Match each state change (melting, freezing, boiling) to its temperature for water.
activities.intendedInsight: Each material has its own change temperatures. For pure substances like water these are specific readable values (at normal atmospheric pressure); some mixtures, like chocolate, melt over a range instead. Thermometer-reading is a real measurement skill.

activities.title: Check and consolidate: place the temperatures, tell the changes apart
feedback: Confirm matches against the fixed values for water and address any 'steady softening with no particular temperature' thinking about water by pointing to the specific °C (some mixtures like chocolate or butter really do soften gradually).
For the melting/dissolving item, restate the one-substance vs two-substance distinction if needed.
activities.rationale: Recall, matching and sequencing checks consolidate and assess the knowledge; this format reinforces recall rather than letting the learner watch the change track the temperature, so it works best after the bench and hands-on tasks.
learnerActions: Place 0°C and 100°C on a thermometer scale.
Match each state change for water to its temperature (melt/freeze → 0°C, boil → 100°C).
Answer a question distinguishing melting from dissolving.
Sequence a heating timeline: ice → water → steam, with the temperature at each change point.
Explain whether melted ice is the same water, and give the reason.
activities.intendedInsight: The learner can state the fixed temperatures, keep melting distinct from dissolving, and explain change of state as the same material at a readable temperature.

constraints: Keep to physical, reversible changes; avoid heating that burns or cooks (chemical change), per DfE guidance.
The KS2 core is observe-and-measure; the particle-level 'why' (heating gives particles more energy to move) is a light bridge to KS3, not the main objective.

A recall/matching/sequencing check reinforces and assesses knowledge but does not let the learner see the change occur at the temperature; pair it with the interactive bench and real hands-on measurement.

A tap-to-reveal annotated timeline consolidates and labels change points but does not drive the temperature to show the change happening at it; treat it as a static scaffold that can still teach the change points.
Fixed change temperatures (water 0°C/100°C) assume normal atmospheric pressure; state this assumption.

The material examples (chocolate, iron, oxygen) illustrate that change temperatures vary; iron/oxygen/boiling values are read/research examples, not precise figures to memorise or materials to handle at those temperatures.
A real thermometer, ice and gentle warming is the natural partner to any on-screen model; the on-screen version is a model of the real measurement.

The 0°C plateau demonstration requires a genuine melting ice-and-water mixture; without remaining ice the reading will not hold at 0°C, and the on-screen bench should mirror this holding behaviour for coherence.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and no medium-superiority or hands-on-necessity efficacy has been established.

Legacy claims that 'live coupling is what a static medium cannot show' and that 3D 'adds no conceptual value' are catalog-fit judgements, not efficacy findings; softened to scoped affordances/limits. A static image or timeline can still teach the change points.

The phrase 'energy first goes into changing state, not raising temperature' (latent heat) is correct for a melting substance held at its melting point; the ice beaker must be a genuine melting ice-and-water mixture for the 0°C plateau to appear, as stated in the activities and constraints.

The bench activity was adjusted so the thermometer reading holds at the change temperature during melting/boiling, matching the real-thermometer plateau task; without this the two scenarios would conflict.

Molten iron, condensed oxygen and boiling water are not suitable for literal classroom handling; treat extreme-temperature materials as read/research examples, consistent with the standard's 'measure OR research' wording.
The assess field frames the particle explanation ('particles move more') within the 'correct answer'; retained as a light bridge only, not as the KS2 mastery criterion.

The NGSS reversibility claim is attached to the bench activity, whose model explicitly demonstrates reversal (re-freeze/recondense); it is not used on the fixed-temperature table activity, which it would not directly support.

assess.poeTask: Put a thermometer into a beaker of crushed melting ice and warm it gently, reading the temperature aloud. Ask the child to PREDICT what the thermometer does WHILE the ice is still melting, and WHY, before you start. Most predict it climbs steadily. It STICKS at 0°C until all the ice has melted, then climbs. The prediction's reason is diagnostic — a child who expects a steady climb hasn't grasped that the energy first goes into changing state, not raising temperature.
probeDeeper: If I melt the ice then refreeze it, is it the same water? How do you know?
Is melting the same as dissolving? What's different about them?
Chocolate melts too — is melted chocolate a new material, or the same chocolate?
When water freezes, does cold go INTO it, or does heat come OUT of it?
assess.correctAnswer: It's the same water — melting is a change of STATE (solid to liquid), not a change into a new material; cooling reverses it back to ice. Ice melts at 0°C and water boils at 100°C. Heating adds energy so the particles move more and the solid becomes liquid.

errorPatterns.pattern: Melting = dissolving — 'the ice dissolved into water'; the two processes are treated as the same.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast: melting needs only heat and involves one substance changing state; dissolving needs a SECOND substance (a liquid the solid spreads into) and no heating is required.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Uses 'dissolve' for ice becoming water in a warm room; can't say how melting and dissolving differ.

errorPatterns.pattern: Change of state = new material — melted ice is thought to be a different liquid from the ice it came from.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Freeze the melt-water again to recover the ice, and note the mass is unchanged — same material throughout, only the state changed.
errorPatterns.distractor: When ice melts it turns into a completely new liquid.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies that the melt-water is the same water as the ice.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Cold moves in' — freezing explained as coldness entering the water rather than heat energy leaving it.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reframe as energy: heating ADDS energy (melt, boil), cooling REMOVES it (freeze); 'cold' is just less heat, not a thing that moves in.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the freezer 'puts cold into' the water; treats cold as a substance.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks melting makes a new substance or is the same as dissolving; has no fixed temperatures for the changes.
responseLevels.full: Explains melting, freezing and boiling as reversible changes of state of the SAME material at fixed temperatures, driven by adding or removing heat energy, and distinguishes melting from dissolving.
responseLevels.partial: Knows melting/freezing and the 0°C/100°C values, but is shaky on whether the material stays the same, or confuses melting with dissolving.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'Two children argue about melting ice. One says when ice melts it turns INTO a new liquid; the other says it's still exactly the same water, just changed state. Who is right, and why?' Then: 'At what temperature does ice melt, and what temperature does water boil?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The 'new liquid vs same water' choice separates a change-of-state understanding from a substance-change belief; the temperature question checks the specific mastery criterion. A child who thinks melted ice is a new liquid, or who confuses melting with dissolving, is exposed by the tier-2 reasoning.
